title: #11 Two good follow-up questions to ask after a diagnostic question
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton's tip addresses what a teacher does after a diagnostic question has been answered correctly by most of the class — the moment where thinking usually stops. His mantra is that the correct answer is not the end of the thinking, and he offers two follow-up challenges that use the distractors as teaching material. The first asks students to explain why someone might have chosen each wrong answer and how they would convince that person otherwise, run first independently on mini-whiteboards and then in pairs before selected pairs report back. The second, more demanding challenge asks students to change the original question as little as possible so that each wrong answer becomes correct. Barton is explicit that the 'as little as possible' constraint is doing the pedagogical work: it keeps attention on the concept at the heart of the question rather than letting students drift into unrelated territory. He illustrates with a simple arithmetic item — what is 10 more than 43 — showing that 44 becomes correct under '1 more than 43' or '10 more than 34'. The tip closes by noting that both challenges are generic: they work with any diagnostic question, whole-class or with a subgroup while others complete the original task.
points: The central pedagogical claim is that distractors are underused assets — explaining why a wrong answer is tempting probes understanding that a correct vote conceals.
The minimal-change constraint is the precision instrument here, forcing students to stay on the concept under test rather than inventing a loosely related question.
The independent-then-paired-then-public sequence is a deliberate participation structure, giving every student thinking time on a whiteboard before any reasoning is shared aloud.
Both challenges are content-agnostic and reusable, which makes them a routine a teacher can attach to any existing diagnostic question rather than a one-off activity.
The differentiation move is quiet but practical: the follow-ups can run with a confident subgroup while the teacher supports students still working on the original item.
quotes: Last week we discussed diagnostic questions in terms of developing good habits. This week I want to share my mantra that with a diagnostic question, the thinking does not need to stop with the correct answer.

The vast majority of students vote that the answer is B. Sure, we could move on, but we could also probe our students' understanding by turning their attention to the incorrect answers. Here are my two favourite follow-up challenges:
Why might someone think the answer was 44? How about 430 or 52? And how would students convince someone that they were wrong?

Students could think about this independently first, writing thoughts down on mini-whiteboards, and then engage in a paired discussion to compare their reasoning. And then you can call on some pairs to share their thinking.

As little as possible is the key here. This ensures you are assessing students’ understanding of the concept at the heart of the question, and not allowing their attention to wander into different realms of the subject.
These two challenges can be used with any diagnostic question. They can be used whole-class, or with smaller groups of students whilst you support others with the original question.
